newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German workers take to streets on sick pay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German workers take to streets on sick pay.

text.p: More than 100,000 workers across Germany walked out on Tuesday to protest against major companies implementing a controversial new law aimed at cutting the corporate burden of paying for sick-pay.

About 100,000 workers at industrial group Daimler-Benz AG alone were expected to have participated by Tuesday night in protests at more than 50 group sites around Germany, the Daimler works council said.
Some 10,000 Mercedes-Benz workers demonstrated outside a company plant in the Stuttgart area against the new policy of Daimler, parent company of the luxury carmaker.
Union officials said workers, upset at the new law from Bonn that cuts sick pay to 80 percent of gross pay from the prior level of 100 percent, then went home for the day.

Mercedes workers, which last weekend began stopping production at the main plant in Stuttgart, were joined in solidarity by about 600 delegates from the OeTV transport and public transport union and other union representatives.
"Sick pay is no luxury. We are not swimming in money like the top managers," Helmut Lenze, the Daimler works council chairman at a Mercedes plant in Stuttgart, told the rally.
Other major carmakers in Germany faced similar actions.
At Ford Motor Co's main factory in Cologne, about 12,000 workers stopped work during the early shift to attend a rally to press the company to explain what it intended to do on sick pay.
About 9,000 workers at other Ford plants owned by the U.S. carmaker were scheduled to hold demonstrations on Tuesday.

Another 7,000 workers at the Bochum plant of Adam Opel AG, a unit of U.S. carmaker General Motors Corp, also laid down their tools to attend a rally and protest at Opel's plans to implement the new law from the start of November.

But some companies on Tuesday reached compromise over the sick pay issue, which has threatened to create widespread labour troubles for Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his push to make Germany financially healthy for the single European currency.

Carmaker Audi AG, a unit of Volkswagen AG, said its workers will receive 100 percent sick pay but that 20 percent of time lost will be put into "time accounts" in which workers will accrue "time debts" to be worked off or paid back.
Electronics giant Siemens AG also said it had agreed with its works council to continue making full wage payments to workers in the event of illness.

The new law, approved as part of Kohl's austerity plan aimed at whipping Germany's finances in shape for currency union, aims to trim 12 billion marks ($7.88 billion) of wage costs which companies claim make them uncompetitive in world markets.
But unions have argued that the measures would cost an average employee who was sick for one month about 500 marks and leave them with additional costs to pay for healthcare.

Kohl has largely stayed out of the conflict except to insist the new law should be implemented in a way that does not break existing wage agreements. He has not yet said whether companies with the new policy are breaking wage deals.
Mercedes' Lenze said Kohl, who has criticised Germans for exploiting Germany's comfortable social benefits, of "laying the foundations" for the new law.
He said Daimler, the first major German company to put the new law into practice without consulting worker groups and unions, was applying the "personnel policies of Rambo".
"We promise the Daimler board that this is only the beginning," he told workers, confirming that overtime and weekend shifts would not be worked until Daimler backed down.

Gerhard Zambelli, the regional head of the powerful IG Metall union, also said he had received confirmation from Daimler management that the industrial giant would cancel existing agreements on Christmas and other bonus payments.
"There have got to be more cuts... To think otherwise would be naive," he said.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($1=1.5231 Mark)
